title: Should the Weekend Bus Pilot Expand?
description: Paired arguments about whether pilot evidence is strong enough for a larger transit commitment.
subject: rla
passage:
SOURCE A - Transit Planning Office

The city should expand the Route 18 weekend pilot from Saturday-only service to both Saturday and Sunday for one year. During the twelve-week Saturday pilot, average boardings rose from 310 to 468 per Saturday after buses began running every thirty minutes instead of every hour. A rider survey collected on board found that 44 percent of respondents were traveling to work and 27 percent were traveling to shopping or medical appointments. The planning office also reports that missed-trip complaints fell from an average of 19 per month before the pilot to 7 per month during it.

The office estimates that Sunday service would cost $186,000 for a year. It argues that Saturday results justify the expansion because many employers, clinics, and shopping centers operate on Sundays as well. The proposal includes quarterly review: if average Sunday ridership remains below 180 boardings after the first six months, the service could be reduced or ended. The office acknowledges that Saturday ridership does not guarantee equal Sunday demand, but it argues that a monitored trial is the best way to measure it.

SOURCE B - Budget Review Committee

The city should not commit to a full year of Sunday Route 18 service based on the Saturday pilot alone. Saturday boardings increased, but two changes happened at the same time: buses became more frequent and the city temporarily reduced the weekend fare from $2.00 to $1.25. The pilot data therefore do not show how much of the increase came from frequency and how much came from the lower fare. The fare has since returned to $2.00.

The committee also questions whether Saturday travel patterns can be transferred directly to Sunday. Several large employers along Route 18 operate reduced Sunday shifts, and one clinic on the route is closed Sundays. Instead of a one-year expansion, the committee recommends six Sundays of service at the normal fare. It would compare boardings by hour, count riders left waiting at major stops, and ask riders about trip purpose. If use is strong, the city could then authorize a longer trial with better evidence about actual Sunday demand.

Both groups agree that weekend access matters and that the Saturday pilot improved service reliability. Their disagreement is about what the existing evidence is strong enough to justify now: a monitored one-year expansion or a smaller Sunday test first.

The planning office adds that the Saturday pilot ran through both school weeks and a holiday period, which gives it more variation than a one-day test. The budget committee responds that seasonal variation is exactly why six Sunday test dates should be spread across different weeks rather than held consecutively. It also asks the transit office to report the cost per boarding, not simply total ridership, so the council can compare Route 18 with other weekend services. The planning office agrees that cost per boarding is useful but cautions that a new Sunday route may need time to become familiar to riders before early numbers stabilize.

questions.prompt: Which source presents the stronger argument for the specific question of whether Sunday demand is already known well enough to justify a one-year commitment?
questions.explanation: Source B addresses the central evidence gap directly: actual Sunday use under the normal fare has not yet been measured.
questions.rule: For argument strength, judge which source handles the most important uncertainty with relevant evidence and reasoning.

options.text: Source A, because increased Saturday ridership automatically establishes Sunday demand.
options.whyWrong: Saturday use is relevant but the passage identifies different Sunday employers and clinic hours.

options.text: Source B, because it identifies limits in transferring Saturday results to Sunday and proposes a direct Sunday test before a longer commitment.
Source A, because any proposal with a quarterly review is stronger than a shorter pilot.
options.whyWrong: A review is useful, but it does not erase uncertainty about the size of the initial commitment.

options.text: Source B, because transit programs should never be expanded without perfect evidence.
options.whyWrong: Source B supports testing and possible expansion; it does not demand perfect certainty.

questions.prompt: What is Source B's strongest challenge to using the Saturday ridership increase as causal evidence for more frequent buses?
questions.explanation: Because two meaningful changes occurred together, the data cannot isolate the effect of frequency alone.
questions.rule: When a policy changes several variables at once, causal conclusions need evidence that separates them.

options.text: The pilot lasted twelve weeks.
options.whyWrong: Duration alone does not identify the main causal problem.

options.text: Many riders traveled to work.
options.whyWrong: Trip purpose does not isolate why total ridership increased.

options.text: The fare was reduced at the same time frequency increased, creating another plausible cause of higher ridership.
Sunday service would cost money.
options.whyWrong: Cost affects the decision but does not explain the Saturday increase.

questions.prompt: Which point do both sources accept?
questions.explanation: The final paragraph explicitly identifies shared acceptance of access/reliability benefits while locating the disagreement in the next evidentiary step.
questions.rule: Find the shared premise beneath the policy disagreement.

options.text: Sunday ridership will exceed 180 boardings immediately.
options.whyWrong: Neither source knows actual Sunday demand yet.

options.text: The reduced fare should become permanent.
options.whyWrong: The fare issue is discussed only as a confound.

options.text: A full year of Sunday service is the only reasonable next step.
options.whyWrong: Source B recommends a smaller test.

options.text: The Saturday pilot improved some aspects of weekend transit, but additional evidence can help judge Sunday service.

questions.prompt: Which evidence would most strengthen Source A's case for moving directly to the one-year Sunday trial?
questions.explanation: This evidence directly addresses the transfer problem identified by Source B while matching current fare and destination conditions.
questions.rule: The strongest added evidence targets the opponent's best objection, not a side issue.

options.text: Recent counts showing substantial Sunday travel demand at major Route 18 destinations, collected at the normal fare and during normal employer/clinic schedules.
A statement from the planning director that Sunday service feels necessary.
options.whyWrong: The director already supports expansion; another assertion does not close the Sunday-demand gap.

options.text: A list of every bus stop on Route 18.
options.whyWrong: Stop locations do not establish Sunday demand.

options.text: The original Saturday rider survey repeated on another Saturday.
options.whyWrong: More Saturday evidence would not directly measure the disputed Sunday demand.

questions.prompt: How do the two proposed tests differ in evidentiary risk?
questions.explanation: This comparison recognizes the tradeoff rather than treating either design as automatically superior in every respect.
questions.rule: Good source comparison can identify tradeoffs even when one argument is stronger for a particular decision.

options.text: Source A gathers no data, while Source B gathers data.
options.whyWrong: Source A includes quarterly review and ridership thresholds.

options.text: Source A gathers more real-world data but requires a larger initial commitment; Source B reduces the commitment but may provide a shorter and potentially less representative sample.
Source B guarantees an accurate annual ridership estimate because six Sundays are always enough.
options.whyWrong: A six-Sunday sample can still be affected by weather, events, and seasonal patterns.

options.text: The two proposals have identical costs and durations.
options.whyWrong: One is a one-year service proposal; the other is six Sundays.

questions.prompt: Which summary best captures the disagreement?
questions.explanation: The summary preserves each source's recommendation and the evidence logic behind it.
questions.rule: A synthesis should state the real point of disagreement and the reasons on both sides.

options.text: Both sources oppose Sunday service but disagree about bus fares.
options.whyWrong: Both are open to Sunday service; they disagree about the evidentiary threshold for expansion.

options.text: Source A argues that promising Saturday results justify a monitored one-year Sunday trial; Source B argues that confounding changes and different Sunday conditions justify a smaller direct test first.
Source A relies only on surveys, while Source B relies only on costs.
options.whyWrong: Both sources use operational and ridership evidence.

options.text: The sources disagree over whether Route 18 exists on Saturdays.
options.whyWrong: Saturday service is an accepted fact.

curriculum.learningObjective: Evaluate claims, evidence, reasoning, and multiple sources under GED-style conditions.
